In the Hudson River estuary, hatchlings of Atlantic sturgeon emerge from the demersal, adhesive eggs after an incubation period of approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] when water temperatures average 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C]. Newly emerged larvae are lecithotrophic, depending entirely on their yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth for these prolarvae has been estimated at around 0.0082 grams [Wwb = around 0.0082 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 2.5 millimeters observed in this species. This modest initial mass underscores the vulnerability of the early larval stages. Growth during the first weeks is rapid as the larvae transition from yolk absorption to active feeding on zooplankton. The temperature dependence of embryonic development is pronounced, with hatching success and larval condition closely tied to thermal regimes in the nursery habitats. Juveniles eventually disperse into the lower estuary and coastal waters.

As individuals progress toward adulthood, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before initiating gonadal maturation. The onset of puberty in females has been documented to occur at approximately 8 years since birth [tp = approximately 8 years since birth], a figure reported for populations inhabiting waters averaging 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Males reach this developmental milestone somewhat earlier, with puberty recorded at roughly 7 years since birth [tp = roughly 7 years since birth] under similar thermal conditions. This substantial sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is common among acipenserids and reflects the greater energetic investment required for female gamete production. Prior to attaining reproductive maturity, juveniles occupy benthic feeding grounds where they prey on macroinvertebrates and forage fish. The extended prepubertal period allows for the accumulation of the substantial body mass needed to support the high energetic costs of reproduction.

The maximum reported lifespan for wild Atlantic sturgeon is notable among anadromous fishes, with individuals reaching at least 60 years [am = 60 years] of age under the thermal conditions typical of the northwestern Atlantic, approximately 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Coupled with a delayed onset of reproduction, this extended longevity contributes to a relatively slow life history pace. The maximum wet weight attained by adult females, recorded at 202,400 grams [Wwi = 202,400 grams], ranks among the highest in the family Acipenseridae, reflecting the species' slow growth and high energetic investment in somatic tissue, which is typical of long-lived acipenserids. This large body size is associated with a substantial ultimate total length. For females, the maximum recorded length reaches 430 centimeters [Li = 430 centimeters], while males are typically smaller, with an ultimate total length of 403 centimeters [Li = 403 centimeters]. Such values position Atlantic sturgeon as one of the largest freshwater-spawning fishes in North America. These life history traits render the species particularly sensitive to anthropogenic mortality.

Reproductive output in Atlantic sturgeon is considerable, with individual females capable of producing between 0.4 and 8 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 0.4 and 8 million eggs per spawning event] when maintained at water temperatures near 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This high fecundity per event, however, is balanced by an extended interval between spawning migrations. Females typically participate in only a single spawning event every 3 to 5 years, corresponding to a reproductive frequency of about 0.2 to 0.33 events annually [F_R_i = about 0.2 to 0.33 events annually]. The energetic demands of vitellogenesis likely contribute to this low spawning frequency. Males, in contrast, may join spawning runs more regularly, though their reproductive allocation per event is considerably lower. The cumulative lifetime reproductive output of this species, shaped by iteroparity and long lifespan, is nevertheless substantial.

The migratory ecology of Atlantic sturgeon involves extensive movements between freshwater spawning grounds and marine feeding areas. Adults exhibit strong philopatry, returning to natal rivers for reproduction. The temperature regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] appears to be a critical threshold for multiple life history processes, including the onset of spawning migrations and the pace of gonadal recrudescence. Physiological studies indicate that resting metabolic demands scale allometrically with body mass, with large adults requiring substantial prey intake to meet annual energy budgets. Anthropogenic pressures including habitat fragmentation, bycatch in coastal fisheries, and historical overexploitation have led to population declines across much of the species' range. Contemporary conservation efforts focus on restoring connectivity to historical spawning sites and reducing incidental mortality. Long-term field studies continue to refine estimates of growth rates, age structure, and demographic parameters vital for population modeling.
